text: City of Fremont Charter Advisory Committee Special Meeting April 6, 2026 5:00pm – 7:00pm City Council Chambers 3300 Capitol Avenue, Building A Fremont, CA The public is invited to participate in the Charter Advisory Committee meetings and provide comments on agenda items or matters within the Committee’s jurisdiction. Public participation may be in person or remotely. For remote participation, the meeting will be available for viewing (1) live stream and may be viewed on the City of Fremont’s website at www.Fremont.gov/Channel27, which also provides a link to the live stream; (2) on Comcast Channel 27 for Comcast cable subscribers; or (3) via Zoom https://us06web.zoom.us/j/82674545723; Webinar ID: 826 7454 5723. The public may also attend the meeting in-person in the Council Chambers; the lobby doors open approximately 15 minutes prior to the start of the meeting. The public is strongly encouraged but not required to wear masks. Submission of Public Comments: For those wishing to make public comments at the April 6, 2026 Charter Advisory Committee meeting, you may either: (1) submit your comments by email prior to the meeting, or (2) by Spoken Public Comment during the meeting. How to submit Public Communications/Public Comment by email prior to the meeting: Send an email to councilmeetings@fremont.gov by 1:00 p.m. the day of the meeting. Please identify the agenda item number and meeting date in the subject line of your email or specify that it is not related to an agenda item. Emails will be compiled into files by agenda item number, distributed to the Charter Advisory Committee members and staff, and published in the City's Agenda Center on www.fremont.gov. Electronic comments on agenda items for the Charter Advisory Committee meeting may only be submitted by email. Comments via text and social media (Facebook, Twitter, etc.) will not be accepted. How to provide Spoken Public Comment during the meeting: Attend meeting in-person in the Council Chamber, fill out a Speaker Card, and submit to the City Clerk. This Special Meeting is called pursuant to the Ralph M. Brown Act (Government Code § 54956) and business is limited to the item listed on this agenda. A single Public Comment period will be provided during the meeting for any item on this agenda. Each speaker may speak once. No public comment will be taken other than as noted in the agenda. Generally, the order of discussion after introduction of an item will include staff comments and information (if applicable), followed by Committee questions, then public comment, and then deliberation and action by the Committee. Items on the agenda may be moved from the order listed. If you are an individual with a disability and need a reasonable modification or accommodation pursuant to the Americans with Disabilities Act, or if you do not have access to email or the internet, please contact the City Clerk’s Office at (510) 284-4060 or cclerk@fremont.gov at least two business days prior to the meeting for assistance. Your responses to this form are not intended to bind you to any official decision or recommendation, but they will help the Charter Advisory Committee determine if there is a consensus around key questions.  Council-Manager (maintain the current City of Fremont’s general law structure)  Council-Manager (charter city)  Strong Mayor  Mayor-Council  Standards: The mayor votes on all council agenda items.  Ties: The mayor only casts a tie-breaking vote.  Veto: The mayor has veto power.  Yes  No any way? If so, why? Questions from 3/30/26 Meeting: ➢ How does city staff currently support the Mayor and City Council? And how does this relate to Item (I)(G) regarding Interference in Staff Functions in the Council Handbook? ➢ The City of Fremont is a Council-Manager form of government. The City Council sets the policy of the City, including adoption of a budget and legislation deemed necessary by the City Council but does not direct staff other than the City Manager and City Attorney. The City Manager serves as the administrative head of city government and executes the policy of the City Council, enforces the legislation adopted by the City Council, and directs all subordinate officers of the City. The Fremont Municipal Code, specifically section 2.10.090, requires the City Council to deal directly with the City Manager and to refrain from giving orders to subordinates of the City Manager. This protocol is common in cities that operate under a CouncilManager form of government and is referred to as a “Councilmanic Interference” provision. The City Council, as a body, directs the City Manager and this provision is intended to prevent individual council members from improperly involving themselves in the administrative or executive functions of city management. The City Council Handbook includes a similar provision. In sum, in a Council-Manager form of government, a city council does not direct any city employees that are subordinate to a city manager. It is important to note that this does not prevent City staff from providing a wide variety of support to the Mayor and City Council. ➢ The Mayor and Councilmembers may request support from City staff currently through the City Manager or City Attorney. For example, the Mayor may need assistance with talking points for an event and will ask the City Manager, who will direct appropriate staff to support this. Or, a City Councilmember may have a constituent question or concern, which they will share with the City Manager, who will direct staff to respond to the inquiry. These are examples of support that occur on a daily basis. ➢ What are some of the consequences of changing the form of government or granting the Mayor or Council additional hiring authority? ➢ Greater political influence over operational issues, and specifically hiring, could impact the nature and stability of key positions in the City organization. As a local example, since 2000 when Oakland transitioned to a strong mayor form of government, the City has had 8 permanent City Administrators and 5 interim (temporary) City Administrators. ➢ It’s also worth noting that a change in the form of government may not result in higher performance across a range of important indicators. In comparing the 5 California cities that are strong Mayor-Council with Fremont across key indicators such as crime rate, poverty rate, bond rating and unemployment, Fremont performs best in all categories, except unemployment, where it performs second best to San Francisco. This is why Fremont is consistently ranked as ‘Happiest City’ and one of the best cities to raise a family in national surveys. ➢ What is meant by ‘hybrid’ form of government? ➢ The term “hybrid” does not denote a particular form of government. The surveyed charter cities refer to themselves in their charters as one of the following forms of government: (1) Council-Manager, (2) Mayor-Council, or (3) Strong Mayor. The term “hybrid” is a colloquial term that has been used to describe governments that blend features from these models. For example, “hybrid” can refer to a Mayor-Council form of government where a mayor is a chief executive of the city, but executive power is shared with the city council (e.g., the mayor appoints a chief administrative officer, but the appointment is subject to confirmation by the city council). Or the term hybrid can be used to describe a Council-Manager form of government where additional authority is provided to the city council such as appointing or confirming the appointment of department heads. To avoid confusion, presentation materials will continue to describe the three forms of government found in charters. ➢ What are the potential costs of developing a City Charter and specifically, pursuing a change in the form of government? ➢ Depending on the nature of the Charter or the extent of change in government that occurs, the costs could vary significantly. However, the most likely direct costs would be related to the Charter placement on the ballot, the potential addition of staff, and increased Mayor/Council compensation (as identified in the City Council Charter Work Plan). i. Election Cost - $611,000 - $855,000 (ONE TIME) ii. Direct Staff for Mayor & Council –Estimate of $149,089 - $1,043,623 (ONGOING, based on a range of 1-7 Management Analyst I positions, total compensation. Note this figure could adjust depending on what level position is filled.) iii. Increased Compensation for Mayor/City Council – Data to be provided at 4/13 Committee Meeting (ONGOING) ➢ What are the sources and requirements for transparency and accountability that the City must currently adhere to? ➢ California local government officials are governed by several laws that address transparency and accountability. Key laws include the following: i. The Ralph M. Brown Act – The Brown Act is a law intended to ensure the public’s right to attend the meetings of public agencies, facilitate public participation in all phases of local government decisionmaking, and curb misuse of the democratic process by secret legislation. ii. The Public Records Act – The Public Records Act provides the public the right to inspect or obtain copies of governmental records, upon request, unless there is a legal basis not to do so. iii. Conflict of Interest Laws – California conflict of interest laws prohibit government officials from making or influencing decisions that financially benefit them, their families, or their business interests. Persons holding specified public offices are required to file disclosures of investments, real property interests, and income within specified periods of assuming or leaving office and annually while in office. (Political Reform Act and Government Code Section 1090). iv. Campaign Contribution Disclosure Laws - California has an extensive framework for transparency as it relates to campaign contributions. In addition, Chapter 2.30 of the Fremont Municipal Code is the local campaign contribution ordinance that limits campaign contribution is local elections and requires the filing of election campaign statements.
